items.prompt: A platform team wants several accounts in one AWS Organization to use a shared Transit Gateway without duplicating the network resource. Which service is designed for this sharing model?
constraints: The resource supports AWS RAM sharing.
The accounts are managed in one Organization.
The team wants centralized ownership of the shared resource.

options.text: Use AWS Resource Access Manager to create an organization-scoped resource share and keep the Transit Gateway owned by the network account.
Create identical Transit Gateways in every account because network resources cannot be shared.
Put the Transit Gateway ARN in an IAM group because groups provide resource sharing.
Use an SCP to grant each account ownership of the central Transit Gateway.

feedback.Reason: AWS RAM is the AWS service for sharing supported resources across accounts, OUs, or Organizations while retaining resource ownership.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A resource share names supported resources and principals. For organization sharing, the owner can share with the Organization or selected OUs/accounts, and the resource remains owned by the sharing account.
Details.scenarioApplication: The network account creates the share, the member accounts accept or receive the share according to organization settings, and attachment permissions are governed separately.
Details.errorCorrection: Duplicating resources is unnecessary, IAM groups do not share infrastructure, and SCPs restrict permissions rather than transfer resource ownership.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: RAM centralizes resource lifecycle and can reduce duplication, but the owner must manage availability, quotas, routing, and consumer offboarding.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Supported resources can be shared through RAM without duplicating each resource.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: IAM groups collect identities and policies; they do not share network resources.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: SCPs do not grant ownership or implement resource sharing.

items.prompt: A central account should share a subnet only with accounts in the Production OU, not with every account in the Organization. Which RAM principal scope is most precise?
constraints: The subnet is a supported RAM resource.
The Production OU contains only intended consumers.
The share should adapt when accounts enter or leave that OU.

options.text: Share the resource with the Production OU and review the inherited consumer set when accounts move between OUs.
Share with the entire Organization because OU membership is not a RAM principal scope.
Share with Principal '*' and use a subnet route table to identify accounts.
Share with the management account root and assume all members inherit subnet access.

feedback.Reason: RAM supports sharing with an OU, which matches the requirement and keeps membership aligned with organization hierarchy changes.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A resource share can target an Organization, OU, or account where supported. An OU target includes its accounts according to RAM and Organizations behavior, so account moves affect the effective consumer set.
Details.scenarioApplication: The network team uses the Production OU target and monitors account placement and resource-attachment permissions.
Details.errorCorrection: Organization-wide sharing is broader, wildcard sharing is unsafe, and management-account ownership does not implicitly grant member access.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: OU-scoped sharing simplifies lifecycle management but makes OU governance part of the network access boundary.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Sharing with the entire Organization includes accounts outside Production.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: RAM principal scope, not a route table, controls which accounts receive a share.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Member accounts do not automatically inherit a management account's RAM permissions.

items.prompt: A team creates a RAM share in us-east-1 but consumers in eu-west-1 cannot see the shared regional subnet. Which property should be checked first?
constraints: The resource is regional.
The share is configured in one Region.
The consumers use the RAM console in another Region.

options.text: Confirm the share and consumer view use the resource's Region because regional RAM resources are not globally visible from every Region.
Change the subnet to a global resource by attaching an IAM policy.
Assume RAM is unavailable for VPC resources because all VPC resources are account-local.
Move the consumer account to the management account because Region determines organization membership.

feedback.Reason: RAM sharing visibility and resource scope depend on whether the resource is regional or global and on the Region used to manage the share.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Regional resources are shared and discovered in their Region, while global resources have a different RAM home-Region model. A subnet is regional and cannot be made global by IAM policy.
Details.scenarioApplication: The operator opens RAM in us-east-1, validates the share status and consumer account, and confirms the VPC resource is in the expected Region.
Details.errorCorrection: IAM policies do not change resource geography, VPC resources can be shared when supported, and organization membership is independent of Region.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Regional sharing requires explicit multi-Region operating procedures when a platform spans Regions.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: IAM policies do not change a subnet's regional scope.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: AWS RAM supports sharing of supported VPC resources.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Account hierarchy and Region are separate concepts.

items.prompt: A workload account uses a shared resource but wants to change its configuration. What must the architect distinguish?
constraints: The resource remains owned by the central account.
The consumer account has permissions to use the resource.
The team must not assume use implies ownership.

options.text: RAM sharing grants supported consumer access, but the owner retains lifecycle and ownership responsibility unless the service documents a separate consumer permission.
The first consumer automatically becomes the resource owner after accepting the share.
The consumer can change any owner policy because RAM converts resource policies into identity policies.
The management account becomes the owner of every resource shared through RAM.

feedback.Reason: RAM provides access to a shared resource without transferring resource ownership to the consumer account.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The sharing account owns the resource and controls its lifecycle, while consumer permissions depend on the resource type and service model. RAM does not rewrite ownership into an IAM identity policy.
Details.scenarioApplication: The platform team documents which operations consumers may perform and routes owner-level changes through the central account.
Details.errorCorrection: Acceptance does not transfer ownership, RAM does not convert resource policies, and the management account is not automatically the owner of all shared resources.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Central ownership reduces duplication but creates an operational dependency on the owning account's availability and change process.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Consumers do not become owners merely by accepting a share.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: RAM does not convert resource controls into identity policies.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Resource ownership stays with the account that owns the resource, not automatically the management account.

items.prompt: A security service supports an Organizations delegated administrator. Why would a company use that model?
constraints: The management account should avoid operating every security service directly.
The delegated account is approved for the service.
Organization-wide visibility remains required.

options.text: Delegate supported service administration to a designated member account while retaining organization-level governance and oversight in the management account.
Delegation gives the member account ownership of the AWS Organization itself.
Delegation removes the need for SCPs because the member account becomes the root account.
Delegation means every AWS service automatically shares its control plane with the member account.

feedback.Reason: Delegated administration separates service operations from organization ownership without changing the Organizations management-account boundary.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: AWS services that support Organizations delegation can designate a member account to administer that service across the organization. The management account retains organization responsibilities and must review the delegation.
Details.scenarioApplication: The platform team registers the approved security account as delegated administrator and protects the organization management account from routine service operations.
Details.errorCorrection: Delegation does not transfer organization ownership, make a member account root, or apply automatically to unsupported services.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Delegation improves separation of duties and reduces management-account use but adds another privileged account to govern and monitor.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: The management account remains the organization owner.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Delegation does not remove organization policy boundaries or create a root account.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Delegated administration is service-specific and requires supported integration.

items.prompt: A company needs a tamper-resistant audit record of management activity across all member accounts. Which CloudTrail design best fits?
constraints: The trail must cover the organization, not one account only.
Logs should be centralized in a protected log archive account.
The team needs multi-Region management events.

options.text: Create an organization trail that applies across member accounts, sends logs to a protected central S3 destination, and enables the required Regions and event types.
Enable CloudTrail only in the management account because member-account events are automatically included in every local trail.
Store audit logs only on an administrator laptop because S3 storage can be modified by members.
Use VPC Flow Logs alone because they contain all API caller and policy-change events.

feedback.Reason: An organization trail provides centralized coverage for member-account management activity and can deliver evidence to a protected log archive.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: CloudTrail organization trails can apply across an AWS Organization. Central S3 storage, restrictive bucket and KMS policies, retention, and multi-Region configuration support audit durability.
Details.scenarioApplication: The security account owns the log archive, the organization trail is centrally governed, and auditors can query events without member-account write access.
Details.errorCorrection: A management-account local trail is not a substitute for organization coverage, laptops are not durable audit storage, and VPC Flow Logs are network telemetry rather than complete API history.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Central trails improve evidence consistency but create storage, access-control, and event-volume cost that must be planned.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A local trail in the management account does not automatically collect all member-account events.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Local copies on a laptop are neither centralized nor tamper-resistant evidence.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: VPC Flow Logs do not replace CloudTrail API event records.

items.prompt: An auditor asks for evidence of IAM, Organizations, and Control Tower configuration changes. Which CloudTrail event class is the starting point?
constraints: The changes are control-plane API calls.
The organization trail records management events.
The auditor needs caller and request metadata.

options.text: Search CloudTrail management events in the central trail and correlate eventName, userIdentity, account, Region, and eventTime.
Search only S3 data events because IAM and Organizations changes are object-level operations.
Use CloudWatch metrics alone because metrics include the complete request parameters.
Use VPC Flow Logs because policy changes are network packets between accounts.

feedback.Reason: IAM, Organizations, and Control Tower configuration changes are management-plane activity captured through CloudTrail management events when configured and supported.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Management events record control-plane operations such as creating, updating, or deleting resources and policies. The event includes identity and request context useful for an audit timeline.
Details.scenarioApplication: The auditor filters the central trail for the relevant service event names, account, Region, source identity, and time window, then links events to approved changes.
Details.errorCorrection: Data events are for resource data operations, metrics do not contain complete request evidence, and VPC Flow Logs are not API audit records.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Management-event capture provides broad governance evidence, while data-event capture should be added where object or function access auditing is also required.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: S3 data events cover object operations, not general IAM and Organizations control-plane changes.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Metrics summarize behavior and do not replace event details and caller identity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: VPC Flow Logs do not record policy API requests.

items.prompt: A governance team wants one view of whether encrypted EBS volumes and required tags comply across all accounts and Regions. Which service pattern is appropriate?
constraints: The team needs resource configuration state and compliance rules.
Accounts and Regions are numerous.
The central team should not manually inspect every account.

options.text: Use AWS Config rules in the relevant accounts and Regions with a central aggregator for organization-wide compliance visibility.
Use CloudTrail alone because CloudTrail continuously evaluates resource configuration compliance.
Use RAM because resource sharing automatically evaluates encryption and tags.
Use an SCP to report current resource state because SCPs are configuration inventories.

feedback.Reason: AWS Config evaluates resource configuration against rules, and an aggregator provides a central view across accounts and Regions.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Config records configuration items and evaluates rules for compliance. A Config aggregator collects compliance and configuration data from multiple accounts and Regions for delegated governance visibility.
Details.scenarioApplication: The central team deploys or enables the required Config rules, configures aggregation, and routes noncompliance to remediation owners.
Details.errorCorrection: CloudTrail records events rather than continuously evaluating current configuration, RAM shares resources, and SCPs restrict API permissions.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Config improves configuration evidence but incurs recording and evaluation cost and depends on complete account and Region enrollment.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: CloudTrail is event history and is not a continuous configuration compliance evaluator.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: RAM has no general encryption or tag compliance engine.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: SCPs are policy boundaries, not resource configuration inventories.

items.prompt: An auditor asks whether a workload was prevented from creating an unapproved resource and whether an existing resource later drifted. Which evidence pairing is strongest?
constraints: The organization uses preventive and detective controls.
The auditor wants both attempted prevention and current-state evidence.
The account is enrolled in central governance.

options.text: Use CloudTrail for the attempted API event and preventive-policy result, then use AWS Config or Control Tower status for current-state and drift evidence.
Use only the current Config item because it proves whether the creation attempt was blocked.
Use only an SCP document because it proves that no resource ever violated the policy.
Use a billing invoice because charges identify the exact denied API request.

feedback.Reason: Prevention evidence and current-state or drift evidence answer different audit questions and should be correlated.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: CloudTrail can show an API attempt and caller context, while Config evaluates resource state and Control Tower reports governance drift or control status. A policy document alone does not prove runtime outcomes.
Details.scenarioApplication: The auditor builds a timeline from the API event, control decision or error, resulting Config evaluation, and any remediation record.
Details.errorCorrection: A current state cannot prove a blocked historical attempt, an SCP text cannot prove runtime compliance, and billing is not API authorization evidence.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Multiple evidence sources improve assurance but require synchronized retention, access control, and clear event-to-resource correlation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Current configuration does not prove a past denied request.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Policy text shows intended control, not every runtime outcome or drift event.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Billing data does not identify complete denied API context.

items.prompt: A finance team needs cost reports grouped by business unit across accounts, while security needs OU-based guardrails. Which combination provides both dimensions?
constraints: Accounts can have stable business-unit metadata.
OU hierarchy expresses governance and lifecycle.
The requirement is reporting plus preventive policy scope.

options.text: Use account tags or equivalent account metadata for cost grouping and OUs for inherited governance policies; do not use one as a substitute for the other.
Use only OUs because OU names automatically become cost allocation tags for all billing systems.
Use only CloudTrail event names because they determine business-unit cost ownership.
Use a VPC route table because network topology is the authoritative account classification.

feedback.Reason: Account metadata and OU hierarchy serve different purposes: reporting classification versus inherited governance scope.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Organizations supports account hierarchy and account metadata, while billing tools use cost allocation and account tagging mechanisms according to their supported model. OUs determine where organization policies inherit.
Details.scenarioApplication: The finance team defines a controlled business-unit taxonomy and the platform team places accounts in OUs based on lifecycle and security posture.
Details.errorCorrection: OU names do not automatically replace every cost-allocation mechanism, CloudTrail is evidence rather than billing classification, and network routes do not define governance ownership.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Maintaining two taxonomies requires reconciliation rules, but conflating them creates either weak governance or misleading cost reports.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: OU hierarchy is a governance structure, not a universal replacement for cost allocation metadata.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Event names do not define cost ownership.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Network topology is not the canonical account governance taxonomy.

items.prompt: A member-account administrator must not be able to delete centralized CloudTrail logs. Which architecture best protects the archive?
constraints: The log archive is in a dedicated account.
The organization trail delivers logs to S3.
Security investigators need read access without broad write access.

options.text: Use a dedicated log archive account with restrictive S3 bucket and KMS policies, separate administrative roles, retention controls, and organization-level governance.
Store the logs in each member account so every member can verify and delete its own copy.
Allow all member-account administrators s3:DeleteObject so they can correct bad events.
Disable log delivery after the first incident to prevent future tampering.

feedback.Reason: A separate log archive account and restrictive resource policies reduce the ability of workload administrators to alter centralized evidence.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The S3 destination and KMS key policies can deny deletion or key use to member-account principals while granting controlled delivery and investigation roles. Organization trails and retention settings provide broader governance context.
Details.scenarioApplication: The archive account separates delivery, investigation, and administration roles and tests that a member administrator cannot delete or rewrite objects.
Details.errorCorrection: Member-local copies increase tampering risk, broad DeleteObject undermines evidence, and stopping logs removes visibility rather than protecting it.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Central archive protection adds account and key-management complexity but is necessary when the evidence must outlive member-account incidents.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Member-local storage is easier for a compromised member administrator to alter.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Broad delete permission defeats tamper resistance.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Disabling logging worsens incident evidence and does not prevent prior tampering.

items.prompt: A project account is removed from the Production OU but still appears to use a shared network resource. What should the owner review?
constraints: The share targeted the Production OU.
The account was recently moved.
The owner needs to prevent unintended continued access without breaking other consumers.

options.text: Review the RAM share's current principal resolution, consumer attachment state, and service-specific resource permissions after the OU move.
Delete the entire Transit Gateway because any OU move invalidates all RAM shares.
Change the member account's root password because RAM access is tied to root credentials.
Ignore the account move because RAM principal membership is fixed at share creation.

feedback.Reason: OU-scoped sharing and resource attachment state can change the effective consumer population, so lifecycle evidence must be reviewed rather than assumed.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: RAM resolves organization principals through account and OU membership, while the resource service controls how consumers attach or use the shared resource. A principal move does not necessarily revoke every existing attachment automatically.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner checks the share, account membership, attachment, and network route state, then removes the consumer or updates the share through an approved process.
Details.errorCorrection: Deleting a shared central resource is destructive, root passwords are unrelated, and share membership is not a one-time immutable list.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: OU-based sharing reduces manual share updates but requires offboarding and account-move review.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A single consumer lifecycle event does not justify deleting a shared central resource.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: RAM resource sharing is not controlled by a member root password.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Organization and OU principals can resolve as account membership changes.

items.prompt: A detective control reports that an account is noncompliant, but the application is still serving traffic. What is the correct governance interpretation?
constraints: The control is detective rather than preventive.
The finding is current and actionable.
The application owner needs continuity while remediation is assessed.

options.text: The control detected a state after it existed; the team should contain or remediate it through an explicit workflow rather than assuming detection blocked the workload.
The workload cannot be serving traffic because every detective finding automatically denies all requests.
Delete the account immediately because detective controls cannot provide useful evidence.
Ignore the finding until the next billing cycle because detective controls are informational only.

feedback.Reason: Detective controls identify noncompliant state but do not necessarily prevent or automatically remediate the underlying operation.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: AWS Config and related controls can evaluate existing resource configuration and report compliance. Remediation may be automatic or manual depending on the designed workflow; detection alone is not a preventive deny.
Details.scenarioApplication: The platform team assesses service impact, applies a supported remediation or containment action, and records exception approval if immediate repair would threaten availability.
Details.errorCorrection: A detective finding does not imply traffic was blocked, account deletion is disproportionate, and ignoring a finding discards a governance signal.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Detective controls support broad coverage but require response ownership, remediation automation, and exception time limits.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Detective controls observe and evaluate state; they are not automatically preventive denies.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Account deletion is not a normal response to a remediable configuration finding.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A detective finding is actionable evidence, not merely an irrelevant informational message.

items.prompt: An auditor asks why a member account lost access to a shared network resource after a governance change. Which timeline is most useful?
constraints: The resource is shared through RAM.
The account was moved between OUs.
A central SCP and CloudTrail organization trail are enabled.

options.text: Correlate the account move, new inherited SCPs, RAM share membership and attachment state, the denied API event, and any approved remediation record.
Use only the current OU name because it contains the entire history of access changes.
Use only the VPC route table because policy changes cannot affect shared resource access.
Delete and recreate the share so the audit starts from the current compliant state.

feedback.Reason: The failure can arise from the interaction of hierarchy, organization policy, resource sharing, and runtime request evidence, so the timeline must join those sources.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: An OU move changes inherited organization policies, RAM principal resolution can change consumer eligibility, and CloudTrail records the resulting control-plane and access events. Current state alone cannot establish causality.
Details.scenarioApplication: The auditor builds a protected sequence from Organizations, RAM, CloudTrail, and remediation records, then distinguishes intended governance from accidental drift.
Details.errorCorrection: OU names do not retain complete history, route tables do not replace authorization evidence, and recreating the share destroys useful chronology.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Cross-service timelines take more operational discipline but are essential for explaining multi-account access changes without broadening permissions blindly.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Current hierarchy is state, not a complete history of the access change.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Network routing and policy authorization are separate evidence dimensions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Recreation discards the original share and remediation history.
